utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good morning to you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. And good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm Patricia Sellers for the Prosecution. With us today is co-counsel Ms. Joanne Richardson and also our case manager Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink. And good morning to the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, I'm Vasvija Vidovic, appearing with Mr. John Jones on behalf of Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us our legal assistants, Ms. Adisa Mehic and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you and your team. So I take it there are no preliminaries. Let's bring the witness in and start. You have 15 minutes to finish, to conclude, Ms. -- I see. If we leave the transcript as it is it may gave us an indication that I have forgotten your name. So it's Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hogic. Welcome back. We are going to continue and hopefully finish. Yes, Ms. Sellers, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hogic.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to be brief in some of your answers. I think you understand we are under a little bit after time constraint. Yesterday we spoke a little bit about the military police and I would like to ask you some questions about the security or intelligence service. Was that part of the service that was constructed within 2 Corps?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The military security service existed as a sector. It was headed by an assistant commander. There was also another sector, intelligence-related issues, also headed by an assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you briefly say what was the function of that service.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The function of the security service was to carry out measures of a security nature throughout the area covered by the 2nd Corps. I think someone else might be better placed to give you an answer to that because I myself was no member of the security service and it's difficult for me to speak about their full range of task. At any rate, their role was to preserve security and order within the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps. Security-related affairs constituted an entirely different area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were there members of this security service attached to various units, companies, battalions, platoons, brigades, within the 2 Corps structure?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Security officers occupied the relevant positions for security, starting at battalion level and up the chain, brigade, operations group and corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would they be subordinated to the commander of a brigade level or whatever level that they were attached to?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they were subordinated to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Maybe you can help us with this. Among their functions, would it be the questioning or interrogation of prisoners, prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move to my final area. Mr. Hogic, yesterday you testified that you gave advice to commanders who faced situations where members of their units might have or did commit crimes or disciplinary infractions; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, what steps could a commander initially take if they knew or if they suspected that a member of their unit had committed crimes?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was a commander who learned in some way that one of the members of the unit under his command or those within the 2nd Corps had committed a criminal offence, and this commander would go to the security bodies to ask for an investigation to be opened into what exactly had been done. Having learned whether the case in point was a mere infraction or a criminal offence, further steps would be taken. If it was just an infraction, then there would be disciplinary measures at the level of the unit. If there was a crime that was committed, then the district prosecutor's office would be informed and this district prosecutor's office would then press charges before a the relevant court. And this is the sort of advice that we always gave the commander whenever he faced a dilemma as to what should be done when soldiers under his command committed acts that had an element of criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like Mr. Hogic to look at the screen. We are going to show a short video clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could know which exhibit this is because it may than we have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Sellers, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: This is an exhibit, this is part of an interview that was taken by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, we strongly object to this witness being asked to comment on interviews with, particularly if it's with our client, making statements about someone else has said. And Your Honour it may be the witness should stand down because of course this did appear on the exhibit list. We weren't sure if the Prosecution was going to try and show this interview. But the fact is, as Your Honour will no doubt recall, when my colleague sought once to put to a witness that someone, a certain named person had said something, Your Honour intervened and said no no, that's not the way to do it you shouldn't say who said something. You can merely say if someone were to say such and such what would your reaction be. If you show an interview then it's obvious that the person -- it's doing the same thing but in a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That would be another witness. This is -- this time, as I take it it's the accused himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This wasn't another witness. Your Honour, I think perhaps the witness should stand down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think it's best to ask the witness to leave the courtroom for a short while and we need to determine this. Please, it will only be a couple of minutes. I'm sure you understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it Ms. Sellers is going to refer the accused to an interview with the accused -- the witness to an interview with the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What I'm going to do is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is different from -- the accused is different from any other witness who has or will be taking the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, may I pass up -- I hope Your Honour won't prejudge the issue before I've made the submission. The last situation didn't involve a witness either. It involved Mr. Deronjic, who isn't a witness in this case. Can I pass up, if I may, with the usher's assistance, pass up extracts from that hearing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you know as much as I do, Mr. Jones, that whatever the witness may have said in whichever circumstances are extremely relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Relevant, but Your Honour, it's a question of whether this witness -- I trust that Your Honour will hear me out on this one but we would hate to see one rule applied against us and one rule --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's different. You have enough experience to distinguish between the accused and anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour if I may refer to you what happened there, my learned friend asked the Chamber -- she was going to read two brief parts of the interview given by Mr. Deronjic to the Office of the Prosecutor. Again, precisely the same circumstances, interview by someone to the Office of the Prosecutor. You said I'll quote: "No, no, no, this is not the way to do it." The witness stood down. Then Your Honour went on: "I had to stop you because the way to do it is precisely along the lines that was raised by yourselves earlier on. The practice is or shouldn't be or it's not desirable that you tell the witness who said whatever you're going to put to him." And that -- just stopping there, Your Honour, that's a general comment. There is no exception for the accused. "You select whatever you want to put to the witness without telling him who said that. You just put to the witness what do you have to state as regards the following statement or would you agree with the following statement, but you don't tell the witness who has made that statement, on what occasions, et cetera." And then further down at the bottom of the next paragraph, "But you don't tell him this has been stated to us by Mr. Deronjic or whoever." And then when the witness came back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones I think I have to cut you on this because I absolutely see no similarity at all between the case you're mentioning, any other case which may involve a third person and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour may I put it this way: Why does the witness need to know that the accused said something? Why can it not simply be put to him what if someone were to say such and such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because you're not the Prosecutor in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But Your Honour, that principle which Your Honour applied in one circumstance against us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Listen Mr. Jones, if you don't like it you have a right to appeal later on but this is our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whatever the accused may have said on other -- in other circumstances, the Prosecution has a right to bring forward and to put questions to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour I have two additional points on there subject aside from what Your Honour ruled before, I do fear a double standard is being applied, but I will reserve the right to appeal.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. I'll slow down. There are two other issues -- well, in fact there are a whole host of issues arising from the interview with the accused. Firstly, the Prosecution so far in this trial has not done what I would expect, really, in any national system as regards the interview. Namely to bring evidence that this interview was conducted, that it was conducted under proper circumstances without threats, coercion, with his rights having been read to him. Rather than just inviting you to look at a piece of paper or a video clip when you've got know assurance whatsoever, no evidence before you that any of the safeguards against abuse that exist in any civilised country, any civilised system, have been observed. That's firstly. Secondly, our client was interviewed for about two weeks. He said a great number of things and of course the Prosecution is going to pick the plum and leave the duff and simply extract one sentence or a few phrases out of this whole mass of material and out of context and ask Your Honours to have regard to that. Now, in our submission, it's not possible for Your Honours only to -- only to have regard to one part of an interview. That means either Your Honours will have to hear the whole interview, read the whole interview, or certainly undertake that you're going to watch the video or read the transcript, which comprises two lever arch files. And we would absolutely insist on that and I'm sorry to have to insist because how otherwise can it be fair to the accused that the Prosecution selects a few random phrases or sentences out of this whole interview and puts that before Your Honours? Thirdly, as far as this witness is concerned, this witness was not in Srebrenica at any time. He wasn't present for this interview. He can't properly say what was going through our client's mind when he said certain things. So in fact, it's clear there is no real desire on the part of the Prosecution to put any meaningful question to this witness which couldn't be meaningfully put by simply say what would you say if someone were to say X. In fact, it's a surreptitious way of getting parts of the interview before Your Honours. It's completely unhanded I would submit and inappropriate way to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to object to any language where the Prosecutor is now being said to be underhanded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Underhanded. I agree. I agree with you, Ms. Sellers. MS. SELLERS I would ask that learned counsel sell would be a bit more judicious in the selection of his words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers. You're perfectly right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That cuts both ways, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour I would object to that refrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Have you finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Only to say this: That if this witness is or if the Prosecution is permitted to put parts of the interview, then obviously we have an equal right to do the same and we will do the same. It will prolong the proceedings but we will put to him selections from the interview as well. We will say here is our client saying X, Y and Z and I'm sure the witness will say I can't say what's going through his mind because that's what any sensible person would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I see that out of the about five minutes you have taken, 4 and three-quarters have been gratuitous assertions, Mr. Jones. You ever drawn conclusions based on assumptions and nothing else. The Prosecution have a right to conduct their own case the way they like, provided it's within the parameters of the law. They will be allowed to make use of this video, to put any questions they like. I don't know if the video in its entirety is going to be tendered in evidence or whether it has been tendered in evidence. That much I don't know. Has it been tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour the entire video has been tendered in evidence. The entire transcript, the revised transcript has been tendered in evidence. And I believe that it is part of the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It makes it instead of 4 minutes and three quarters, it's the entire five minutes were gratuitous assertions on your part, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the matter stands. Please sit down and let's close the matter here. The Prosecution has a right and I will not -- we will not interfere with the Prosecution's right to put questions to witness on prior statements of the accused -- in particular prior statements of the accused. It's unheard of in any jurisdiction that there will be objections entertained along these lines. If you then want to make use of this video, do so by all means. We are not going to stop you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Will Your Honours read -- watch the whole video and read the whole transcript? Will you give that undertaking?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will do -- listen, we will not take instructions from you, Mr. Jones, what we will do or not. If it's in evidence we will see it, I can assure you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The whole of it. Good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's bring the witness in, please. I wouldn't expect you even to hint that we are the kind of judges that we will not review an entire video if it is in the record, as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, my case manager has just reminded me. We will be putting the transcript, the hard copy into today. The video has been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We haven't seen the video, obviously, but we will see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers, your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour I would like to hand up the transcripts at this point. This is Prosecution Exhibit P329.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This is an extract. It needs to be made clear this isn't the whole interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Counsel is quite correct. This is an extract just for purposes of today so that we could have the transcript on page 12 we will be referring to for this first part. The entire transcript, certainly, will be furnished. And we agree with our learned friend's submission that we have taken small parts, given our time limit, given what is relevant to this witness, that these are excerpts and we invite any broader view or look at the transcript certainly to be given. Your Honours, if I may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. And you've got ten minutes to conclude all this, Ms. Sellers, now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic you've just testified about steps or measures that or advice that would be given to commanders if they knew or suspected that members of their units had committed crimes. I would ask you now to look at the small clip that will be on the video in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "UNIDENTIFIED SPEAKER: Because Ramiz was the person who was close to the military structures and he knew what the procedure was. "UNIDENTIFIED SPEAKER: [In English] military structures and he knew the things that should be -- "UNIDENTIFIED SPEAKER 1: [Interpretation] The same applies to Hamid Salihovic. "UNIDENTIFIED SPEAKER: [In English] [Previous translation continues]... but I just told that that I don't remember, I didn't remember this order and the various things that were in it. But I also signed a lot of things that I didn't even read. I told you at the beginning that as far as paperwork and things were concerned I didn't pay much attention to that, and I wasn't thinking very much about the Geneva Convention or the Tribunal. My main aim was how to save the Muslim people in that area, how to remain -- and how to remain and survive in that area. "UNIDENTIFIED SPEAKER: [In English] Perhaps let me ask him another way."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, very briefly for questions of time I'd like to show a following clip to which these transcripts pertain. And page 2 will be the relevant part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really have an objection here. The Prosecutor selected only one limited bit on the video. It's quite clear that he's talking about a document. It is quite obvious that he's not talking about his own order on how his soldiers behave in accordance with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. Finish. Sit down, please. You know what the rules are. You can object but you cannot try to influence the witness. Yes, let's see the next part of the video and then your question, Ms. Sellers, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "UNIDENTIFIED SPEAKER: [In English] How can I possibly agree when as I've said I didn't know anything about these cases. The only case that I knew about was the man who died or rather was killed by Mirzet. I have no idea whether there were any of this these prisoners or where any of these prisoners were. This was the responsibility of Hamid Salihovic. "I was -- I was the commander and according to some -- according to some rules, I should have been aware, but I was -- we were being pressed on all sides by the Chetniks and it was much more important for me to be on the front lines, protecting the front lines, than to worry about what was happening down there. There were people there who were responsible for what was happening there. "So I have no idea either who they were or where they were or even if indeed they were these civilians. "The ones that I remember -- the ones that I remember were the one that is I've told you, that is there was Vlade [phoen], in the first instance, there was the three from Podravanje. There was the two from Fakovici. There was the woman with her child who later married Hazim, and then from Kravica there was the two, one who was wounded and later died, and the other who was healthy. Those are the ones I know about."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, my question is: Based upon the advice that you gave commanders in the past, if they knew or suspected that a member of a unit had committed crimes, in the clips you have seen would there be sufficient information for a commander to take those steps that you've outlined?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This witness is being asked to pronounce on what -- essentially on some of the ultimate issues in this trial but on the basis of already an out-of-context extract from an interview, whether that information hypothetically would be enough to put a commander on inquiry, that's eminently a question for Your Honours. It's not a question for had this witness. It's a hypothetical. He doesn't know what information our client possessed. He doesn't know whether -- in fact he knows nothing at all about the situation that's bean described. He's being asked to address a hypothetical. It's for Your Honours to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not hypothetical at all, Mr. Jones. It's very clear. The question is on the basis of what you have heard here in terms of the instructions that you had given to commanders, what would have been the responsibility of the commander. This is basically the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, if the commander had only that information, would that be enough, in your opinion; that's a hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No it's not hypothetical at all, Mr. Jones. It's not hypothetical at all. It's like a horse on a carriage, one follows the other. Yes, Mr. Hogic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, having heard what Mr. Oric said, given such information, he should have instituted proceedings or taken measures against men suspected of having committed certain crimes. So that is the advice that I as an assistant commander for legal affairs would have given. I would have given such advice to my 2nd Corps commander if he had asked me about such information or anything in this sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any further questions, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, now I'd like to show -- I have one question I'd like to show a final clip and a concluding question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, I just want to ask you, would you confirm that based upon your position as assistant commander for legal affairs, were you -- was the advice that you gave your corps commanders and the members of the ABiH army, was it consistent with that they could not contravene the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like Mr. Hogic to look at this last very short clip, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: For the record we object against that clip for the same reasons. But I know Your Honour will rule against me on that, so --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I think it has another P number, just for purposes of identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the P number of the clips of the video? Were these last two clips --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The last two clips were P329, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: This clip is P432, previously tendered into evidence. I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic my final question is: Was it the position of 2 Corps or, as you described yesterday, other corps, the ABiH army in itself, Bosnia and Herzegovina, but particularly in your capacity as the assistant commander for legal matters, was it the position that a member of the army could choose which provisions or when and where to obey the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was necessary to fully respect the Geneva Conventions, and I think that the command corps did not change its position from the very beginning and right up until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I thank you very much, Mr. Hogic. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Ms. Sellers is now going to be followed by Madam Vidovic. Now, you speak the same language and that usually, from our experience, creates problems in the sense that you tend to follow immediately. Sometimes you don't even allow question and answer to be finished. So what I recommend strongly -- Ms. Vidovic knows about this, I don't need to preach to her, but to you I need to. Please allow a short interval of time between question and answer because whatever you say needs to be interpreted in two other languages to us so otherwise you will make it very difficult for the interpreters to be able to follow. Yes, Madam Vidovic. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, might I just raise one preliminary question and it just might be an oversight on the part of learned counsel but I believe that there are two exhibits on your list that we haven't received yet. So I could just bring that out first. If we could get them during a break prior to their use that would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We also, I think -- Registrar, please. These transcripts I think we need to give them a number and the number must relate to the video. So this last one I don't think we have a transcript for it, but these relate to the previous ones. Okay? So it will be point 1 or point 2, I don't know. If you can mark them for me, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We will convey the time in the clip, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, thank you. Your responsibility is to answer all questions honestly and to the best of your ability, Mr. Hogic. So let's start.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Hogic. I have a lot of questions I want to put to you, yet time is limited and so I will be grateful if you could answer my questions as briefly as possible. If you agree with me, you could just say yes; if not say no, unless the Trial Chamber requests an explanation or unless I ask you for an explanation. I hope you have understood me. Thank you. Mr. Hogic, from the 10th of June 1992 until December 1992, you were the assistant of the chief of the 2nd Corps of the after the ABiH; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that capacity you interpreted the manner in which the legal system functioned and the manner in which the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina functioned, firstly in the municipal Territorial Defence staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were well aware of the way in which the defence functioned and the legal system functioned at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Up until December, 1992, municipal staffs which were part of the Tuzla district were not organised in the way they should have been organised according to the regulations, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly speaking, yes, if I may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, many units in the Tuzla area were organised on an independent basis, they had organised themselves.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The citizens had founded them on their own initiative.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And often they were given quite cute names.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Up until December 1992, there was no system of unity of command and not even in the Tuzla area; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To an extent. I can't fully confirm that claim but you are partially correct, because there were certain differences as far as the functioning of defence concerned with regard to Gradacac, with regard to Brcko, with regard to Sapna and Teocuks [phoen]. There were certain organisational difficulties. And it was only when the corps was established in September 1992 that these difficulties started to be resolved. It was only at the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993 that these difficulties were resolved when operative groups were formed and municipal staffs were treated as separate from corps units.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From December 1992 until April 1993, you were the chief of the legal service of the 2nd Corps of the ABiH; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the title was -- yes, well the title was chief of the legal service.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. So you know how municipal defence staffs should have functioned in accordance with the regulations at the time?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke in detail about commanding the military police and about the units in which the military police was present. Today and yesterday you also spoke about commanding in the organs of military security, and I have a few questions for you about this subject. First I will base my question on a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show the witness document from the Supreme Command staff and we will provide our colleagues from the Prosecution with this document immediately. They said that this is a document that they do not have. This is a document from the Supreme Command staff of the ABiH, temporary formation, number T-412185. It has to do with the municipal defence staff with attached units and the year is 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please first have a look at the first page. And would you agree that it concerns a temporary formation for a municipal defence staff with attached units and the year concerned is 1992?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't have to mean that it's for the entire year 1992. There is a temporary formation which occasionally changes. This may have been in force in 1992 but until the subsequent changes were made, this remained in force.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you are not aware of the fact that there were some other kind of temporary formation in 1992 apart from this one?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as this formation is concerned, it had to do with defence staffs and attached units, and the personnel sector of the 2nd Corps command was responsible for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, please answer my question. We will get to that but my question was: This is a municipal staff formation; have a look at the second page.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was issued on the 25th of September 1992. My question was: In 1992, there was no other formation established; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know nothing of any other formation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could you now have a look at that second page once again. Would you agree that this is an order from the chief of the Supreme Command staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was Mr. Sefer at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will now quote, here it says "Pursuant to Article 9, temporary military formation will be established." Could you please have a look at this document and in particular have a look at the last part of the document, page 19. And it says -- well, first have a look at page 19, please. It says that -- it consists of 19 pages and Mr. Avdulah Kajevic certified this; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please now say whether, generally speaking, you would agree that a temporary formation is a document according to which you establish the organisation, the strength, the weapons, the rear supply of a unit or a staff?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, a temporary formation is a -- is the basis upon which you bring units up to strength according to what the supreme -- in accordance with what the Supreme Command staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina regulates; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the military police is concerned, its internal structure, its strength, and the commands and units within which there will be a military police presence, were these things also regulated through such a formation?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: An integral part of a temporary formation is always plan for the organisation of the unit which determines the structure of the unit in accordance with the regulations and decisions of the Supreme Command staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please now have a look at page 7 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version, Your Honours, this is page 10. It's entitled "A Plan for the Organisation of the Municipal Defence Staff, Types 1, 2 and 3." "Municipal Defence Staff Organisation Chart, Types 1, 2 and 3."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please take a look at this chart. We have a commander, you can see the little box where it says commander, then chief of staff, assistant for morale, the security organ, assistant for logistics, financial assistant. And then have a look at what comes under the chief of staff. Please have a look at that part. Have you had a look at the chart?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please now go through the document on the temporary establishment of the municipal defence staff with attached units. Go through the entire document, and please pay attention to the military police. Is the military police mentioned as part of this establishment?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it would be correct to say that this temporary establishment of the municipal defence staff with support units for 1992 did not include the military police as a part of the municipal defence staff? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have an exhibit number for this defence document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Which is the next number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's D272, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To so this document is being tendered and received and marked as Defence Exhibit D272.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now if I could have the usher's assistance, please, I would like to show the witness a different document. The ERN number is 01830897, and this is a document of the Defence Ministry, the Sarajevo Territorial Defence staff, or rather the Defence Ministry of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was signed by the then commander of the Territorial Defence staff, Colonel Hasan Efendic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, if you could please have a look. The title of the document is "Organisation of Military Police Units, Order." I will quote a portion of this document to you now. The introduction reads, "In order to more effectively and rationally carrying carry out tasks within the competence of the military police of the Territorial Defence and regional TO staffs of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina I hereby order: "1. Organise TO military police units at the level of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina TO staff and regional TO staffs." I am quoting the relevant items 3 and 4 now. "3. At the level of regional TO staffs, with the exception of the Sarajevo District Territorial Defence staff, organise a military police unit of the rank of company. It should comprise a command, a section for security -- the security of persons, a section for forensics and investigations, a platoon for securing facilities, and a platoon for anti-terrorist combat." And now comes the part that's particularly relevant to us. It reads, and please pay close attention: "Disband all other TO military police units not organised in keeping with the above items 1, 2 and 3 of this order," which means that military police units of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina must not be established at the municipal level. I want to ask you something about this. Does this document not appear to indicate that at municipal staff levels no military police units were envisaged in this period of time?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite correct. Even if such units had been established, they were to be disbanded, which means that they would have been established contrary to the existing commands and orders issued by the relevant commands.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's true, isn't it, that what was in fact envisaged was for military police units of company level were to be organised at the level of the Territorial Defence staffs, for example the district staff of Tuzla. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was already in early June that we had a Territorial Defence unit established and its name was Balta.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we could please have a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will become Defence Exhibit D273.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now if I can please have the usher's assistance I would like to show the witness OTP Exhibit P143. For the sake of the transcript, this is a document by the district staff of the Tuzla Territorial Defence. The date is 14 of October 1992 and the document was signed by Commander Zeljko Knez.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, now that I've mentioned Commander Zeljko Knez, there is something I'd like to ask you about that before I move on to this document. It's true, isn't it, Mr. Hogic, that the BH army had a considerable number of non-Muslims, that there weren't only Muslims in it?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is certainly correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that it had a large contingent of people in the leading positions, in its highest level organs, who weren't Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, for example Zeljko Knez; then you had Andjelko Makar, who was another Croat. I can't remember all the names now. I was trying to remember a person of Serb ethnicity who also held one of the leading positions in the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, whether we speak about the BH army, we are by no means fair to speak of this army as a Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we'll move on to this document. Please have a close look. I will quote item 1 of this order. It reads: "In the municipal defence staffs of Zivinice, Banovici, Kalesija, Zvornik, Celic, Vlasenica, Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Olovo, and as part of the brigades in the remaining municipalities, military police units shall be set up to the level of a company comprising 105 conscripts. The units shall have a company command, a commander; an assistant for moral guidance, who is also the deputy; a company supplies officer; a driver; a courier; a signals man; and sufficient personnel organised in platoons which shall represent the following, securing features and persons; patrolling; checkpoints; on-site investigations; a crime-prevention service, or unit; an anti-terrorist unit attached to the staff or the brigade." In relation to this, I have several questions to ask you. It's true, isn't it, that on the 29th of September 1992, pursuant to a previous decision of the Presidency dated August 1992, the chief of the supreme -- commander of the supreme staff had ordered the 2nd Corps to be established. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Until as late as the 14th of October 1992, the 2nd Corps had not yet been established. The order you have just seen - if you could please look at the final part of the order again - was signed by commander Zeljko Knez in his capacity as what was still the district staff of the Tuzla Territorial Defence. Wouldn't that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes and no. If I may be allowed to clarify briefly. We received this order by radio link right away to establish the corps. It took effect on the same day, this order and the establishment of the 2nd Corps. Why was the stamp of the district staff of the Territorial Defence used? Or why did Mr. Knez sign this document without explicitly stating his position as commander of the 2nd Corps? Believe me, I don't know the answer to these questions but one thing I can assume is that they had run out of stamps with the -- the official stamps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was for purely bureaucratic reasons that they close this course of action. But there is nothing to suggest that this order or there signature are not authentic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Based on the document that you have in front of you, one might conclude that this commander is giving an order to set up a military -- set up military police units in the brigades, in all the municipalities with the exception of those explicitly mentioned. Wouldn't that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That would seem to imply that on the 14th of October 1992 these municipalities already had brigades established. I'm talking about the one where he ordered the establishment of military police units at brigade level, to be quite precise.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what it means in these municipalities there were brigade level units but there were probably other units too.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. If you could please go back to the document. The commander is providing in this order for an exception in terms of the municipal staff of Kalesija, Zvornik, Celic, Vlasenica, Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Olovo. And I'm about to ask you something in relation to this. The municipalities of Zvornik, Vlasenica and Bratunac were municipalities where the Muslim population had been expelled in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If we talk about the town of Kalesija itself, the Muslim population had been expelled to Dojsic [phoen]. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These municipalities therefore had some sort of improvised authorities and the soldiers from these municipalities were fighting elsewhere, in other municipalities. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The municipality of Celic was, in fact, besieged to the extent that the surrounding Serb lines were at a distance of one or two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think even nearer than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely besieged, yes. Zivince had an open communication to Srebrenica on one side only and the remaining sides of Zivince were also under siege.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, Zivince had no communication with Srebrenica at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore Zivince too was under siege?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. If you go back to the map, you can have a look and see for yourself. Zivince is next to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Witness, yes, you're entirely right. What I meant was that there was only one side to Tuzla that was open and the front line was just next to Zivince municipality. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes that precisely was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the same applied to Banovici?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And Srebrenica was entirely surrounded on all sides. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately you would be very right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These municipalities that we have considered now, on the 14th of October 1992, had no brigades, no established brigades, which was the reason why the commander of the territorial staff of the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence ordered military police units to be set up that were attached to the staffs. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you could please have a look at this document, have a close look, please, and look at the right upper corner. Look at the incoming stamps, please. Witness, you will agree, won't you, that what this document shows is that it, the document, on the 23rd of October 1992 was received in Kladanj and on the 27th of October 1992 it was received by the Kladanj Municipal Assembly. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. That's precisely what the document confirms but it says Municipal Assembly and then there is a caption saying Territorial Defence staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely but there is nothing on this document that appears to indicate that it was ever received in Srebrenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Aside from this remark indicating that it was probably delivered to all the municipal staffs and brigades. You see that at the end of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm asking you is there anything in this document to indicate that it was ever received.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please leave the document with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a very important document and I'll be quoting further sections of this document to have your comment. If you could please look at item 2 of this order, I quote: "The chiefs of security and municipal defence staffs or brigades shall exercise control over military police units in professional terms. While the chief of security of the Tuzla district defence staff or another person he appoints shall check their work and the completion of tasks, and take complete control over the military security service." Item 3 reads: "The selection of military conscripts for the military police units will be carried out by the chiefs of security in the municipal defence staffs and brigade, taking into account the fact that the candidates should first and foremost be those who have served in the army as military policemen. The tasks of the military police and its authorities will be defined by a special instruction from the security organ to the municipal defence staffs." Witness, I have a question to ask you in relation to this. First of all, do you agree that this order draws a distinction between the authority of the chief of the municipal security defence staff on the one hand and the authorities of the chief of the security staff of the Tuzla municipal staff over military police units?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, it draws a distinction between its own superior coming from a superior command and on the other hand the military police unit whose establishment has just been ordered.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If we go back to item 2 of this order, the security chiefs in municipal defence staffs were to be in control of the military police units in professional terms, but their work, the execution of their tasks and everything else, was to be assumed by the Tuzla district defence staff chief of security as a superior on the Territorial Defence municipal level; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we leave the document aside for a moment, please. I will be going back to that document later on but now if I can have the usher's an assistance please I would like to show the witness OTP exhibit P324.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is the rules governing the work of the armed forces security of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from September 1992. You were shown this document by the Prosecutor yesterday for a brief while. Witness, I'm about to ask you a general question about this. You will agree with me, won't you, that these rules governing the work of the military security service were binding for all members of the military security. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you could now please go to this page that bears the number 01837240, so the last four digits are 7240. You will find the chapter marked by the Roman numeral two, in the English version, this is page 5. In the Bosnian version, Mr. Hogic, it's page 4. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The title is, "Commanding the military service department." Now, please have a look at item 11 in these rules. I will quote: "Officers of the military security service in a superior command or staff shall in technical matters control members of the military security service of subordinate command and staffs and shall assist, direct, and coordinate and control their work." Have you read that now, Witness?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Although members of the military security service were officially accountable to -- or rather first of all I will ask you the following. Would you agree with me if I said that the rules regulate the relation you have to superior commands, up to the rank of a corps, and to lower level commands when it comes to the work of the military security? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now my question is as follows: Military security officers, although they were officially within the unit and had to report to the commander of the unit within which they were integrated, these rules on controlling the military security service in fact state that the security organ in the lower level units is controlled by an organ from a high level commander. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't agree with what you said when you said that they were officially responsible to the commander of the -- a military security organ is always materially responsible to its command, its unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We will deal with that.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But in any event, there is this relation of subordination that concerns the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the municipal territorial staff according to the regulations in force on the way in which the security service functioned at the time did not fully control the organ of military security, although he was part of that body. Would you agree with me that the rank of the commander of a municipal Territorial Defence staff is not the same as the rank of a corps commander in relation to the work of the military security service?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this way of putting it is a little complicated. The commander of a municipal staff, when controlling the bodies that are under him, has to make sure that they are used in the best possible say so the Staff Commander had to engage the military security officer as well. But there is another problem, an a factual problem or a legal problem, and that concerns the way in which the security organ functioned in relation to its commander. It is a matter whether it reported more to the commander or to the superior organ of military security.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In accordance with the rules that you have -- that you had a look at and in accordance with the order of Commander Knez for Tuzla -- you still have it before you, and you could have a look at it. The commander of a Territorial Defence staff did not have the authority to control the way in which the security organ functioned and carried out its tasks. This was the responsibility of superior military security commander; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but look, in terms of control, the commander of the municipal staff had the right to control and govern the military security service. But in professional terms, when we are talking about the way in which methods were applied, when we are talking about how the military security functioned, instructions were received from his superior security organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the higher level command?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would you agree with me if I said that only certain levels of command, from the level of a corps commander and above, had the right to have full access to the way in which the military security organ functioned, and this includes the methods it used and the way in which it functioned? This is what you have mentioned. You say certain measures were taken if there were intercepts, if they had recourse to certain other methods when investigating matters. They -- it's only the high level commands that had the right to gain access to such information; would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, again only partially. Think I that certain details concerning the work of the military security were not even details that the commander of the corps was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In other words, as far as the military security service is concerned, it's only the high level commands that had access to knowledge on the way in which though functioned because it's the centre in Sarajevo that was able to gain access to such information and that governed such matters; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, this was Mr. Jasarevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And this is the system of so-called vertical subordination when it comes to commanding the organs of military security. And this was a specific system in relation to other organs and sections of the ABiH; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at a page of the document on rules that you have in front of you. The number is 7247, or that's the last part of the number. On that page, you can see Section 5, the way in which the military security service functioned in criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the pages in the English version are 9 and 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'll quote the relevant provisions, but please first have a look at Article 39, where it says that "the authority in the work of the organs of internal affairs are regulated by the law on criminal procedure, also concerns taking over the actions of authorised officials, in pre-trial and trial proceedings within their field of work." And then we have Article 41. I'll show you item 1. "On the basis of the information gathered, officers of the military security service in the command of the brigade or a corresponding or higher ranking officer in the military security service shall submit a criminal report to the competent military prosecutor's office." I will now read out Article 42. "When the perpetrator of a criminal offence is unknown or when in other cases envisaged by the law, the competent military prosecutor requests preliminary information and/or the taking of other measures, the officers of the military security service to whom the request is addressed is bound to act on it." Would you agree with me if I said that these rules on the way in which the military security service should proceed when criminal proceedings are instituted quite clearly state that communication between authorised officials from the military security service with the prosecutor was direct? So there was direct communication between military security service officials and the Prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher now show the witness document 02622027. That's the ERN number. This is a document from the district military Prosecutor's office in Tuzla, dated the 25th of April 1995, signed by the district military prosecutor, Mr. Alisa Salihodzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please have a look at the document and first have a look at the person to whom this document was addressed.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's addressed to the security department.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it's addressed to the security department, to Colonel Mehmet Zivit [phoen]. Would you agree with that? And it was signed by the district military prosecutor. You can see in this document that the district military prosecutor addressed this document to the security department and this is confirmed -- or rather this confirms that the rule that we had a look at a minute ago, about communication between the military prosecutor and the security organ in fact took place in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said in response to a question put to me by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At levels of command that were lower than the level of a corps, the security organ could but did not have to inform the commander of the unit of which he was a part about action that he took with regard to criminal proceedings; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To a large extent, if I can put it that way. I can't fully confirm that, but you are mostly right because in accordance with these rules, they had the right to investigate certain matters without the commander being aware of the fact because certain matters could be used against the commander himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So an officer from the security organ did not need authorisation from the commander of let's say the brigade or from the staff in order to file a criminal report with the prosecutor, if he suspected that a crime had been committed. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And these rules are quite clear as far as this is concerned; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please give this document an exhibit number, Your Honours? I believe that perhaps we should correct something. I believe that in the English language the date is not correct. The date of the document should be the 25th of April 1995. It seems -- I seem to remember that the date was not recorded correctly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you for pointing that out to us, Ms. Vidovic. In the English version, upper-left corner, where it says Tuzla 25th April 1005, obviously should read 25th April 1995. And this document in its original and its English version, will be marked as Defence Exhibit D274, the English version carrying an E after the number. You have more or less four or five more minutes. Choose yourself whether you prefer to stop now or to continue for the next five minutes and have a break after.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only have two or three brief questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you often present at various meetings in the corps command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the assistant commander of the corps, I was present at all the morning meetings when I was in the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You know, do you not, that the security organ of the Tuzla district territorial staff and the -- until -- and then later the same organ from the 2nd Corps, did not issue instructions or direct the way in which its subordinate organs in Srebrenica functioned; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I don't know how this functioned. Could you be more precise, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you have no information according to which they received instructions from Tuzla, according to which instructions from Tuzla were received in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At this -- during this period of time before the demilitarisation, the legal service that you worked in did not issue instructions of any kind on the way in which the organs of the municipal Territorial Defence staff in Srebrenica should function; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that Srebrenica was isolated, this was quite simply impossible; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it was also because communications with Srebrenica were almost non-existent.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this would be a good time for me to end my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have 25 minutes. We'll start at five minutes to 11. Please try to be as punctual as possible so we try to gain a little bit of the time lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's proceed. Yes, I see Mr. Wubben. What's your problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I have no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You just wants it attract my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Just for the record my name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. Co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers has a short notification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Defence counsel has graciously given me a couple of seconds just to inform you that in terms of the exhibits used last time, P329, it was tape 5 and at that point we were at 39.37 through 41.03 minutes and seconds on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I have two other very briefly. Also at P.329 we were at 7.09 through 9.35 seconds -- minutes and seconds; and that the last tape, which was P432 we were at 22.27 through 22.48 minutes and seconds. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, you testified about the order to apply the provisions of the international law of war that was adopted by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You said that those provisions were binding for all soldiers of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you did not deliver those rules and provisions to Srebrenica before the beginning of 1995, if at all. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You confirmed, didn't you, that General Knez had issued an order on the application of the international law of war?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have no information to the effect that this order was in fact ever delivered to Srebrenica. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you advised the 2nd Corps on the application of the international law of war and that this information eventually reached all the units of the 2nd Corps. But you can by no means claim, can you, that your instructions ever received Srebrenica or at least prior to the first half of 1994, which is when you said you eventually established communication with them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you testified that there were some old laws from before the war in Srebrenica to do with the Criminal Code, as well as some provisions from before the war. In fact, you said probably they had those. I'll ask you something about that. You do know, don't you, that Serb military units occupied Srebrenica between the 17th of April and around the 20th of May, 1992, and that the Serb units devastated the town. You do know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They torched at least 80 houses and homes, they took whatever they could; you're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as the Muslim population returned to Srebrenica following the 20th of May 1992, the refugees occupied all public buildings, including the Court and the Prosecutor's office. Is this something you know about?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They told you themselves, didn't they, that the archive had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that from a number of different sources, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you have no reliable information to suggest that there were in fact any criminal provisions from before the war in Srebrenica, and I mean that the military command had any of these provisions and rules.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was speaking about that as a possibility yesterday, because the Court and the prosecutor's office always had some of the literature in which these provisions were published, such as official copies of the Official Gazette. It was an assumption. They may have been there had they not been destroyed by the aggressor. It's only logical to make that assumption. I'm not sure if they actually had any to consult right there and then. This is not something that I can say.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony you explained the sort of information or, rather, how information on criminal offences passed through the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let us try to keep this simple. When you testified about that, what you had in mind was the military structure of the corps. I mean when you talked about the chain of reporting on possible criminal offences from company level to brigade level, operations group and up to the level of the corps. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me when I say that the structure of the territorial -- of the municipal Territorial Defence staff was in no way like the military structure of the corps which you had in mind when you talked about this?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The functions of the corps as a military unit are different and the military defence -- the Territorial Defence -- the municipal Territorial Defence staff has different functions. It is a territorial body.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Once the corps was established in late 1992, the municipal Territorial Defence staffs continued to exist?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in fact they continued to exist throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, they did not comprise any brigades, did they, within their composition?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You saw the provisional structure of the municipal Territorial Defence staff. You realise, don't you, that they only had attached units, support units, and the so-called territorial units which, for example, might have included an antisabotage unit?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They had no battalions, they had regional staffs that comprised the municipalities, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they covered the municipal territory in terms of military issues and security issues. They secured the territory at the rear of the units that were in operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. These regional staffs provided security for the local communes. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, roughly speaking they would cover one or more local communes each.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance now, please? I would like to show the witness a document. The ERN number is 04033830.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is an order by the command of the 3rd Corps governing the work of military police security bodies. The date is the 4th of February 1993. If you could please have a look. Please have a look at the first line under the word -- under the words, "I hereby order." Do you agree with me that this document is in reference to the order of the Main Staff of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated the 28th of January 1993 speaking about the work of military police security bodies? If you could please have a look at the title of this document.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The work of military police security organs. There is a distinction between drawn between the intelligence and security related matters on the one hand and --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you could please look at item 2 and I have a general question to ask in relation to this. Yesterday, you confirmed that the corps were all applying the same regulations.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had no choice. There were no special regulations that applied to any individual corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's true, isn't it, that the decisions by the Main Staff of the Supreme Command were binding for all the corps including the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will now quote item 2 of this order. It reads: "In the organisation establishment of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina army, military police units are attached to brigades and corps commands. A military police battalion attached to a corps command has territorial jurisdiction in the area of responsibility of the corps, and the brigade police in the area of responsibility of the brigade." I would like now to go on and quote a different portion of this document that's relevant. Item 4: "All members of the military police attached to municipal defence staffs are to be resubordinated to brigades, and if military police brigade units have been fully manned, their military occupational specialty must be changed and they must be reassigned to other manoeuvre or territorially based units." And item 3, which is also relevant: "There must be no military police members in the municipal defence staffs. Regarding military police matters, the municipal defence staffs are to address brigade commands whose military police has been assigned jurisdiction over the municipal territories." Let me ask you something about this. It's true, isn't it, that this document appears to indicate that as of the 28th of January 1993, in terms of the structure and organization of the BH army, there could only be military police units that were attached to brigades and corps commands. Of course when I say brigades, that includes battalions and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're entirely right.
