utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From that point onwards, pursuant to an order by the Main Staff of the Supreme Command of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, members of the military police could not be attached to municipal Territorial Defence staffs if -- even if they had previously been attached to one of these; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the way it should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The order of the Main Staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated the 28th of January 1993, as far as concerns the work of military security bodies was complied with, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, at least as far as the command of the 2nd Corps was concerned. This is a document from the 3rd Corps but I can use it as an example. It jogs my memory about the other order. But as to how these documents were applied by the 2nd Corps, I can tell you that these documents and orders were fully complied with.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You are familiar with the position of the Main Staff when I spoke about the military police, what they said in relation to that, and you fully complied with that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we could please have a number for the exhibit. Again we have a correction to be entered. It's about the date shown here. The date is the 4th of February 1993 in the English and not 1998. Your Honour, it was a quite unclear, the original Bosnian version was somewhat unclear in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic but you have to acknowledge we've made an improvement. Before we were thrown back 990 years and now we have advanced five years. So this will be D275.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned a number of times the Srebrenica Operations Group during your testimony. Can I have the usher's assistance now, please. I would like to show you another document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not clear about whether this previous exhibit has been assigned a number or not. If so, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, there one is 275, D275.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. Your Honours, in fact I'm talking about P31. It already bears the OTP number, which is P31.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, for the sake of the transcript I will say that this is an order of the Main Staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina regarding changes in organisation and the date is the 1st of January 1994. I quote, it says: "Order, Organisational Changes," and then "Establishment. Set up the 8th Srebrenica Operations Group in Srebrenica (the former Srebrenica Armed Forces Main Staff and some of the attached units.)" I want to ask you something about this. If you could have a look please, this order was signed by the deputy brigadier general, Stjepan Siber, on behalf of the commander. And what I want to ask you about this is the following. This is an order of the Main Staff of the Supreme Command on the establishment of the 8th Operations Group and its brigades and it was only issued on the 1st of January 1994. Does this document not appear to indicate precisely that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact you don't know how long it took under the conditions that prevailed in Srebrenica at the time which you spoke about yesterday for this operations group to be set up and you do not know whether it was ever in fact established in full compliance with the provisions.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to say that, the first reason being I was informed about this order and I know that it was produced by the Main Staff of the Supreme Command. I have no idea, though, how it was ever delivered to Srebrenica and whether it was executed. I really don't know. Later, there was an exchange of letters. One thing you must not forget is we are looking at a demilitarised area at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We will be asking you questions about that. We'll get to that later on Mr. Hogic. Thank you. I was just about to ask you a similar question. You do not in fact know what the military structure was in Srebrenica prior to the demilitarisation, if any such thing was in place at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It's basically for the transcript. I think that the answer that Mr. Hogic was about to give and then I believe when Madam Vidovic started to speak -- it looks as if it might have been part of his answer, relating to the demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. We are referring to line 17 basically. Or rather line 16. Or not even that. Anyway you need to look into this later because there a mistake here. Your intervention is included in what he was saying. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Your Honour. The witness said we must not forget about the demilitarisation and my next question was rephrased in order to ask the witness about the demilitarisation so my question is:

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness you do not in fact know what the military structure was in Srebrenica was prior to the demilitarisation, if any such thing as a military structure was in fact in place.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know to the extent that there was information at the level of the command of the 2nd Corps, but that's all I know. I know that there was such a thing as the municipal staff of the armed forces of Srebrenica, that was their name or at least that's what we were told their name was. We always wondered how we should get in touch with these armed forces, how to establish communication and how to get in touch with those units.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you were not familiar with their structure or how the whole thing operated?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think the corps commander himself knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd now like to show you another document, which has to do with the work of the military police in Srebrenica during the period that we have been referring to. I would like you to comment on the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness an extract from P84. 02115050 is the page number, and could we also show the witness the page 02115051. It's dated the 14th of October 1992, Your Honour. The pages in the English version are pages 7 and 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to read out part of the document. The handwriting is not easy to read. I'll read you out part of the page 02115051 and have a look at the part that says "Osmanovic opened the meeting."

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Ms. Vidovic, I have another document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: 5050 is the number. The last part of the number on this page should be 5050. Have you found it, Witness?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Have a look at this part of the document and it says: "The meeting was opened by O. Osmanovic and he said that we were facing problems the functioning of the War Presidency, two staffs - the civilian protection." And I will now read out what follows below that part. "Ramiz intervened and he said the following. The War Presidency replaces the Assembly," and then he said what sort of tasks they had to carry out and then you have the hierarchy referred to. It says, "the War Presidency discusses and assesses the war situation and takes decision. It is the supreme authority and the supreme command. Its command function is carried out through the staff. It is directly under the command of the military police but at the same time the military police are subordinated to the armed forces staff." Witness, I have something I would like to ask you about this. I'm not going to ask you much about Srebrenica, about the situation in Srebrenica. My question is of a legal nature and concerns the field that you were involved in. Throughout the wartime period, you were at the head of the legal service of the corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was the assistant chief from December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The control and command of certain bodies, for example, of the military police, also required that competence or responsibility for the military police be clearly defined. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In order for command to function properly, it is necessary to determine the hierarchy, to determine who is under whom and who is above whom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is a main principle that has to be respected.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This part of the document, of the record from the meeting of the War Presidency of the armed forces staff, it says that the War Presidency has direct command over the military police but the military police is also directly subordinated to the staff. Would you agree with me if I said that here we don't clearly see who is in command of the military police?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally. There is a dual relationship. There are two bodies that have competence, that are responsible, and there is a question or an issue of seniority here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If a body has two commands, then it is difficult to determine the responsibility of those commands for the acts of their subordinates. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please have a look at the next page now. The last part of the number is 50 and 51. Have a look at the page on which Osman speaks. And then in the middle of Osman's speech, you can see certain names that are listed and there are certain numbers. Have a look at number 7. It says, "the chief of the Public Security Service, Becir," and then in brackets we have "(Mirza-military police)" and then it says "Civilian Police, Nurija." Witness, I have a question about this. If - please pay attention to what I'm saying - if the military police was part of the Public Security Service, and it was under the civilian authorities, then according to the rules in force at the time, the commander of the municipal staff could not command the military police. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He could not command the civilian or the military police or the Public Security Service. The commander of the Territorial Defence staff could not have command over such units.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The assistant commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but I think we need to clear this up. If you look at line 8 of the transcript, page -- line 8 of page 51 on the transcript, which is of course a continuation of line 7. Your question was according to the transcript, "The commander of the municipal staff could not command the military police." His answer refers to the commander of the Territorial Defence staff and not the commander of the municipal staff. So I think we need to clear this because the two don't tally. I don't want to let the transcript give the impression that you asked one question and he answered another. You didn't ask him about the commander of the municipal staff. You asked him about the commander of the territorial staff, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Municipal TO staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I will repeat my question. There is very important. Please allow me to repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If the military police was part of the Public Security Service and was under the civilian authorities, according to the rules in force at the time, the commander of the municipal Territorial Defence staff could not have command over the military police; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are quite right. That's the only answer I can give to your question. I want to be quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The assistant commander of the municipal staff or Territorial Defence could not command the military police in accordance with the rules for this service and in accordance with the order issued by Colonel Knez on the 14th of October 1992, if it was under the civilian authorities; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The assistant commander for security could not influence the selection of individuals who would perform duties in the military police if the military police was part of the civilian body; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it wasn't the military police any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have another question for you now. A different question. You would agree with me if I said that regardless of the structures that the military police was part of, the civilian or military structures, in order for it to function at all, it was necessary to have the right personnel and equipment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question is of a general kind about the military police. In order for it to function it had to have the staff and equipment as prescribed in the regulations; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher now show the witness another extract from P84. 02115086 and 5087 are the pages I would like to show the witness. And I just want to quote something from the document. Could you just show the witness page 5086 and under Roman 4 we have Atif Krdzic speaking who says that the military police hasn't been brought up to strength; many have given up because of accommodation; there are no weapons, only two rifles and two pistols; there are three persons missing. And my question is, if the military police is to function properly it was necessary for them to have weapons, insignia, accreditation; would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be ideal that's how things should have functioned, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In order for it to function, it had to have a sufficient number of professional and trained men, organised in platoons, for example, a crime police platoon. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It would have had to have equipment and all the other materiel and technical equipment required to carry out investigations, to question individuals, to ensure that communications functioned. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The usher can remove this document now. We won't need it any more. But as far as this subject is concerned, I have another question for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as you're aware, the district Territorial Defence staff in Tuzla, in the course of 1992 and right up until the demilitarisation in April 1993, cannot have done anything to make the military police unit in Srebrenica function properly, as far as staff and professional men are concerned? The security organ of the 2nd Corps couldn't have done anything?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite right. They couldn't have done anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They couldn't have done anything or rather the military security administration from Sarajevo, as the superior organ, couldn't have done anything either; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your testimony, you mentioned how various stages of the investigation would be reported after a crime had been committed and a criminal report had been filed with the military prosecutor or with any other prosecutor. When you spoke about this, you were bearing in mind the fact that commander -- as a commander and a subordinate commanders, had the equipment that they needed to detect crimes, to carry out investigations, and you had in mind the existence of state bodies that would direct the investigation about which report would be filed with the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If what was called the military police was not sufficiently equipped and trained, was not sufficiently professional, and was part of the civilian structures, then the assistant for security didn't have the means required to detect crimes and to carry out investigations; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Given all those assumptions, your conclusion is quite logical.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the assumptions I have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the assumptions you have mentioned, yes, that's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When they receive information of crimes committed in a given territory -- whether he would receive such information depended on whether such information would be received from someone else, from other sources. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but information can also -- always be received from other sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. That's what I'm talking about, from someone else?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It doesn't have to be received from the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It just depends on that and not on the organ of security. Similarly, would you agree with me if I said that this very much depended on the possibility of such information being relayed in the field itself?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You're aware of the fact, are you not, that up until June 1993 in Srebrenica, there was no prosecutor, nor was there a court with any kind of jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that fact. I also know that there was a decision from the Presidency on relieving judges of their duties, judges who had left Srebrenica and also on relieving prosecutors of their duties. I know that Mrs. Akagic stayed on in Srebrenica. At the time she was either the deputy Prosecutor or the Prosecutor of the municipal prosecutor's office. I know that the judge Hajrudin Halilovic before the aggression itself, left Srebrenica and stayed in Tuzla. Later he was the president of the military court. Now he is again the president of the court in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But let me just ask you the following. Would you agree that there was no prosecutor's office or court until June 1993 there?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not even sure that they were present there after that date either.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But they weren't present there before that date?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no precise information on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, then. If in 1992 and up until the time of demilitarisation in 1993, there was no prosecutor, there was no court, there was no investigative judge present in the area, would you agree with me that it makes no sense to talk about carrying out investigations in terms of the law on criminal procedure that was in force at the time given the conditions that prevailed?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would fully agree with you, but if you remember some of the documents that we had a look at yesterday signed by assistant commanders, these documents referred to certain investigations being carried out and they referred to investigative measures being taken against certain individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, I'm talking about the time before the demilitarisation. Let me be clear. I'm referring to the period before the demilitarisation. I'm referring to the period 1992 and 1993 up to the demilitarisation. You had no information on investigations being conducted, did you?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance now. I would like to show the witness the following document. This is the agreement on demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, please have a look. This is the agreement on demilitarisation. It was signed on the 18th of April 1993 by General Sefer Halilovic and General Ratko Mladic. The ERN number is 01857842. Witness, if you could please look at the relevant section, which is Provision 4 of the document, on page 1. I quote: "The demilitarisation of Srebrenica will be complete within 72 hours of the arrival of the UNPROFOR company in Srebrenica. 1100 hours, 18th of April 1993. If they arrive later, this will be changed. All weapons, ammunition, mines, explosives and combat supplies except medicines inside Srebrenica will be submitted/handed over to UNPROFOR under the supervision of three officers from each side with control carried out by UNPROFOR. No armed persons or units except UNPROFOR will remain within the city once the demilitarisation process is complete. Responsibility for the demilitarisation process remains with UNPROFOR." You have confirmed that you're familiar with the fact that the demilitarisation took place. I have something to ask you about this. This item 4, Provision 4 that I have just read out, implied that the Srebrenica area, the demilitarised Srebrenica area was to be abandoned by all units that could have been described as military units, including the military police and the military security bodies. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the moment the agreement on demilitarisation was announced, there could only be a formal presence of any army in the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is indeed correct, but they would not be allowed to carry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was my point exactly. They would have had to be disarmed. From that moment on, any military presence was illegal in the town itself?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't allowed to be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. UNPROFOR would seize weapons; they even went as far as to search homes in order to find and seize any weapons that were still around; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if you look at a later report, you can see that they even stopped one soldier to seize his weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Any military activity was strictly forbidden with win this demilitarised area; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All in all, if any military presence remained, its function would have been reduced to a bare minimum. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a number for this exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this is being received and marked as Defence Exhibit D276. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now if I can have the usher's assistance please to show the witness a different document. The ERN number is 01838964. This is a document produced by the command of the 8th Operations Group or, more specifically, its security body. The number is 13013-6/194. It was signed by Nedzad Behtic, assistant commander for security and the title of this document is, "Instructions requested." I will quote a portion of paragraph 1 to you in order to save time. It reads: "As you know, Srebrenica was demilitarised on the 18th of May 1993." Truth to tell, it actually states the 8th of May here. "From that moment on, the Srebrenica public security station and the lower court in Srebrenica have assumed responsibility for taking measures against the perpetrators of crimes and misdemeanours. These are military conscripts (members of the 8th Srebrenica Operations Group, military security service) and the military police have not been able to perform their duties as there is no military Prosecutor's office and no military justice in this area and also because it is territorially separated from Tuzla. I would like to point out that cooperation with the Srebrenica public security station is not adequate." In connection with this, Mr. Hogic, does this document not appear to indicate that the military police and the military security service in the Srebrenica area, on account of the demilitarisation, were simply not able to perform their functions as of the 18th of April 1993? Isn't that what the document appears to be saying?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You agree with me, don't you, that under these conditions, with no military police or military police security functioning properly, the commander of the TO staff simply had no means at his disposal, no bodies to use, in order to track down perpetrators of potential crimes or to launch any investigations?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. No weapons, no equipment, no manpower. He would have been unable to do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. To all practical intents, whatever remained of the armed forces of Srebrenica, which had for the most part been disarmed during the demilitarisation, remained stuck in a very small area outside Srebrenica, between Srebrenica, the demilitarised zone and the Serb forces besieging the area. Is this something you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please have a number assigned to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the last document made use of by the Defence is being received and marked as Defence Exhibit D277.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, I'm about to show you yet another document now. This is 130-13-17/94 and the date is the 5th of May 1994. This document was also signed by Nedzad Behtic, and it bears the title "Information Necessary For Future Work." This is a limited document, and I quote -- this is about the Tuzla security sector, and it says: "We would like to inform you that we are unable to complete the tasks you gave us in your communication number SP dated the 24th of April 1994. As you know the Srebrenica enclave is physically severed from the 2nd Corps and members of the military security service do not have any documents or other papers. Likewise we do not have the rules governing the work of the security bodies in the armed forces or any other enactments or decrees governing the work of the security departments in the armed forces. In order to overcome the difficulties in our work and in order to be able to work more effectively, please use the same route to send us copies and amended texts of the said documents and rules. Please send also the forms for identity cards for members of the SVB immediately so that we can start producing these and carry out all of the above orders and tasks." Mr. Hogic, let me ask you this. This document shows that members of what was supposed to be the military police or the military police security in Srebrenica in fact had no documents, had no IDs, or any other decrees or enactments governing the work of all security bodies within the armed forces. Would I be right in stating that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is indeed what this document appears to indicate.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, it's true, isn't it, that at least until the 5th of May 1994, these people in Srebrenica had not received any rules or provisions that they might have used in their work in terms of security and the security bodies, is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words they simply didn't know what to do or how to go about their duties?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is very probable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: There has been a series of speculative questions that no objections were made to asking him did he know things which he said that he didn't have knowledge of the condition in Srebrenica. And I think that counsel should not be permitted to continue that type of speculation. If the document is clear on its face, and we are just commenting on a document, yes; but to ask him did he know about that condition when he stated clearly on the record he didn't know exactly what happened in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But let him testify. He said that is very probable. He didn't exclude it. He didn't speculate. He just said that is very probable. He did give his judgement on this, or his opinion anyway. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, what should have been the military police security, according to the regulations that you're familiar with, if we bear in mind this document, all they had in Srebrenica was the name itself, they were called security body; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and maybe they had a couple of people too.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document now be assigned a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this last document is being received and assigned the following reference number. It's Defence Exhibit number 278. D278, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can the usher please show the witness Defence Exhibit D210. The ERN number is 01838620. It's another document signed by Mr. Nedzad Behtic. The security body, the 10th of September 1994, and it was sent directly to Mr. Enver Hogic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you could please have a look, Mr. Hogic.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. What I have in front of me is an order to a battalion. It says P210.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I said D, D210, not P210. Thank you very much for drawing my attention to this. D. Have you had a look now? The document appears to have been sent to you. It's a very short document and I will quote it. "Pursuant to document number dated the 9th of September 1994, we hereby inform that you we do not have the decree law and special military courts and are therefore asking you to send it to us with its accompanying forms. The names of superior officers to be appointed judges of the military disciplinary court shall be submitted subsequently. Finally we are requesting information on those responsible in cases where a soldier was found to commit an offence outside his line of duty. Whether he would be prosecuted for disciplinary liability or would be a civilian -- would be up to a lower court to decide." Do you recognise this document, Mr. Hogic?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe we received this document in the corps command and it was delivered to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does this document not show in no uncertain terms that as late as the 10th of September 1994, they still had no idea what their competence really was?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The document does demonstrate that in no uncertain terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Also if we look at the document, it shows that they faced a great deal of trouble with soldiers who committed infractions outside their line of duty or what is here referred to as their military duty.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at this document dated the 9th of September 1994, it appears to show that they were not even aware of the existence of any decree laws. They are calling it decree orders or instructions for some reason. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was probably warped [as interpreted] by the information they received so this might have been a misinterpretation on their part. It is quite clear in fact that they did not have a clean text to use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Here, I would go back to the objection that Ms. Sellers raised a few minutes ago, even though she didn't raise one now. But can anyone explain to me how reading the last paragraph of this document, D210, means that the security organ were facing a great deal of trouble with soldiers who committed infractions outside their line of duty? Where does it come out from? I mean -- they are just asking a simple question. What's the position when a soldier commits an offence outside his military duty? It could for all intents and purposes it could be just one case that they had they didn't know how to handle. So this great deal of trouble --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may address the issue. Thank you very much for this suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, I've only just noticed that there is a whole chunk of the sentence that was simply left out in the English translation. In the Bosnian - and if you could please follow what I'm saying, Witness - in the Bosnian original, it reads, and that's precisely the reason I'm asking these questions. "We are requesting information on the respective competencies in cases where a soldier has committed an infraction outside his line of duty. Are disciplinary measures to be taken or would this be up to the lower civilian court?" Which is where my question stems from. They are not familiar with their respective jurisdictions and it appears to be clearly defined in this case. Am I right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're entirely right. If I may clarify the situation just for very general purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's move forward.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So no clarification is required, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you think you owe us a clarification, you may proceed. But to be honest with you, I don't think we need a clarification. It's pretty obvious that there is no indication in the text that the security services there were experiencing a lot of trouble. Yes, Judge Eser has a question for you or for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: For the witness. Now, if these documents and also other documents which we had before talked of decree laws and different regulations and so on, did this refer to the applicability of the Criminal Code or only did it only deal with jurisdictional questions, which means which court, which instance, which organ should deal with these questions? Did it somehow affect in any way the applicability of the criminal provisions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. There could have been two different courts dealing with the application of the criminal provisions. On the one hand you had the regular court and on the other the district military court. As long as we are talking about criminal offences, of course. And this -- in the case of military persons, it could only have been the district military court but not the civilian court. Based on this document it seems that the people in Srebrenica were not clear about this. What precisely does this phrase mean, "a soldier acting outside his line of duty"? This probably means that at this point in time the soldier was not in the unit. He must have been resting or on leave or visiting his family, and during this time he committed a criminal offence. So the question is that is raised at this point is who is responsible for taking further action in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: My question was a completely different one. I wanted to distinguish between the validity of the Criminal Code, whether the Criminal Code had to be obeyed to -- even if there might have been a problem with regard to the jurisdiction which would be at place if a Criminal Code, if a criminal provision, has been violated. I mean, does the question of jurisdiction, which court will have to deal with it, affect at all the validities, the applicability? I mean the question whether you have to obey to the Criminal Code or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite right. It was necessary to respect the provisions contained within the Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, let's clarify something. You have no information according to which in the course of 1992 and at least until the time of demilitarisation in 1993, the decree law adopting the law on criminal procedure was forwarded to Srebrenica; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said you had no information according to which anyone had the Criminal Code in their hands over there.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I know and that's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want to go back to this document. The document quite clearly shows, does it not, that these people from Srebrenica tried to organise themselves? They requested instruction, they tried to establish a military disciplinary court. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In such conditions, they tried to ensure that there was order and they tried to prosecute soldiers that -- who had committed offences.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher now show the witness another document, 04120119. It's a document from the 2nd Corps command, the legal affairs section, dated the 21st of November 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's also addressed to you. Could you please have a look at the document and please have a look at item 6, which I believe to be relevant. It's on the second page. And I'll read it out to you. "In relation to submitting regulations, we are informing you that for the needs of your operations group and the 1st Zepa brigade" -- in fact, Witness, I apologise, this is a document that you drafted and forwarded to Srebrenica. I made a slip of the tongue. Item 6 reads as follows: "In relation to submitting regulations, we are informing you that for the needs of your operations group and the 1st Zepa Brigade, we provided you with a set of official gazettes of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina starting from 1992 until the most recent issue in 1994 which was the 32nd issue which we thought to submit to you by radio. However we have been informed that it is not possible at this moment, due to technical reasons. Therefore we have decided to send you printed material through the UN liaison offices or any of the other humanitarian organisations. We have been informed that this is not the most secure method but we have to try. If we do not succeed in this way then we will send you all the regulations that you need by radio in succession." So this shows that on that date in 1994, they did not have those official gazettes in Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You can also see that these documents could have been forwarded over the radio or rather they could not have been forwarded over the radio given the communications problems, Witness, and the energy supply problems?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the energy supply problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in November and December 1992, after this document was drafted, you weren't able to receive instructions nor were you able to send them to you, given the technical problems that existed? Do you remember anything about this?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: November 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, in 1994.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally. That was the main problem, the communications problems were the main problems at the time we had these official gazettes and they had been downloaded on to the computer's hard disc and we tried to forward them over radio link but it wasn't possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yesterday you said that UN officers and officers from international organisations would not agree to delivering military mail for security reasons; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we assign an exhibit number to this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this last document that has been made use of by the Defence is being assigned the following exhibit number, D279.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher show the witness another document, please. It's a document from the Prosecution. The exhibit number is P540. It was shown yesterday, if that is of any assistance to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, please have a look at the document. It's from the command of the 8th Operations Group in Srebrenica dated the 1st of February 1995, and it was shown to you by the Prosecutor yesterday. It has to do with the analysis of the application of the law for the month of January 1995, and Mr. Hogic please, just have a look at the last part of the document and I will read it out to you. "We would like to request again that you find a way to send the collection of legal regulations concerning the HR, that probably ARB -- and service in the army as many requests in that connection are coming in every day from the brigade commands." It was signed by the assistant Hakija Mehmedovic. Mr. Hogic, this document shows that the legal provisions that concerned the ABiH in Srebrenica -- that these provisions were not available in Srebrenica up until 1995.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hogic, this also includes documents on the military prosecutor and the military court?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher now show the witness another document. This document has the number 01837506, and it is a document from the 8th OG, from the security body. It's dated the 18th of April 1995. Again it was signed by the commander for security Nedzad Behtic and it's called "Overview of the Security Situation." This is the title of the document. This is a lengthy document and I don't have much time so I will read out part of the second paragraph which reads as follows -- It follows on the first paragraph, have a look at it. "Up until this point in time we have received no information from the Srebrenica SJB by demonstrates their attitude and cooperation in this matter." And then there is part of the third paragraph which I will quote. It says -- it starts with the word the process. Can you find that part? It reads as follows. "The process of reorganisation has not yet been completed." Mr. Hogic, could you please have a look at the beginning of the document again? It says the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Command of the 28th Division. And then in third paragraph, it reads as follows: "The process of reorganisation has not yet been completed." The security section, the military police company and other internal organs of the 28th Division have not been fully manned, which if one takes into account the fact that there is no military court or military prosecutor's office in these parts, makes work much more difficult. When one adds to this the fact that many of the officers are not professional and are appointed to inappropriate posts, all this means that the functioning of the RIK system, the commands and control system, has been disabled.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command and control system.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the command and control system. The document shows that the public security station did not respond to the request received from the armed forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since the demilitarisation had taken place, the public security station did not have the duty to provide information to the military command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, this document shows that the organisation of the command and of the units of the 28th Division had not been completed until at least the 18th of April 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what it seems that one could infer from the document. It seems that they were in the process of carrying this task out but it hadn't been completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document also enables one to draw the conclusion that the 28th Division was still just a name on paper. It didn't have the relevant bodies that had been organised in accordance with the regulations; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me to say anything about that. I can confirm what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says on paper.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the document says. But as for the way this was actually organised, so the actual facts, well others could confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this document show that the organ or security section of the military police company hadn't been brought up to strength and that was the case for other bodies within that division? The officials were not -- or rather the officers were not professional, that's what it says in the document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And I have another question for you. When you contacted -- when contacting the corps, the command in Srebrenica mentioned the fact that a military Prosecutor's office and a military court wasn't present in the area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They also mentioned the fact that the officers were not in appropriate posts and were not professional.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And in this document, they also pointed out that it was not possible for the system of command and control to function; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, could we assign an exhibit number to this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that will be D280.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this might be a good time to have a break because I'll be moving on to another subject. If this is not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay, how much more do you have?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I will need another half an hour, Your Honours, but I really will try to complete my examination as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, there will be redirect. I will try to make it as concise as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask everyone to cooperate and make a little bit of a sacrifice and we will have a 20-minute break, instead of the usual break, try to recover a bit of the lost time. I know, but the ones who are working most are the ones behind the -- apart from Madam Vidovic at the moment, yeah, okay. And the technicians? Okay? Yeah, all right. So it will be 20 minutes from now. It's at the moment it's 12.22. So it will be at 12.43. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, I have a few more questions I would like to put to you. Yesterday when you testified about torching, you said that according to the regulations of Bosnia-Herzegovina, setting fire to property was explicitly prohibited; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You would agree with me if I said that any guide books on the armed conflict and the instructions you have mentioned make a distinction between so-called policy of scorched earth and destruction including torching facilities that is justified if this is a military necessity. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you destroy a building that is sniper is using or if there is a tank which is opening fire from the immediate vicinity of such a building; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer that question, please. We've had constant complaints from the Defence while we had the examination-in-chief that the witness is not here as an expert. Madam Vidovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your testimony, you mentioned Ramiz Becirevic, who was in fact someone who completed secondary administration school and had no military knowledge of any sort. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information I had, he was a reserve officer. As to his educational background, his civilian educational background, I know nothing, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You certainly do not know the sort of training he completed as a reserve officer, and you said that you did not know the rank he held.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, upon arriving in Tuzla I was told that he had the rank of captain or major.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that the rank -- one's rank depends on one's level of training?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you do not know the sort of level of military training that he had obtained and I'm also referring to training in international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hogic, can we now please go back to P329. It's an OTP exhibit. This was, if you remember, an excerpt from an interview that was conducted with our client. The video number is 2920. The tape number is 18. And the page is 2. There is a total of 39 pages. I will read the relevant portion to you. This is P329. I believe the witness will remember, but I will still quote the relevant portion in order to save time. "How am I supposed to agree when I know nothing about this? The only thing I agree on, the only thing I know about, is the killing of that prisoner. I mean Mirzet. What I said about these things, I can't remember if they were in fact captured or where they were captured. All these issues were being dealt with by Hamid Salihovic. According to some rules, I was the commander and I was supposed to know. In view of the problems faced by the Srebrenica enclave at the time it was much more pressing for me to be at the front line and to take care of issues on the ground. They had another person down there who was in charge of these issues. So I don't know who they were or where they were or indeed if there were any civilians there. What I do remember is that people were captured, that Radi was captured, three persons from Podravanje, two from Fakovici, this woman from Bjelovac with a child. There was another man who had been brought over from Kravica. One was healthy and the other was wounded and this man later died. And that's as much as I can remember." What I wish to ask you about this is the following: The fact in itself that there were prisoners of war is not in itself a crime. It does not constitute a crime, does it?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, prisoners of war, in the midst of a war, are something that you should only expect, to put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore the existence of prisoners of war does not constitute a crime in itself or the fact that anyone knew of their existence?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that can by no means be defined as a crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There is a reference here to a person named Mirzet. If back in 1992 and all the way to 1993 in the Srebrenica area there was no prosecutor or court, would you agree with me that in that sort of situation, there was no one that could have passed on information concerning the death of this prisoner that is referred to here? There was no court and no prosecutor to pass this information on to.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct. There was no court. Therefore you couldn't inform a court.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Or a prosecutor for that matter.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no way to pass on information. If indeed there was another body, it would have been anyone's obligation, anyone who found out about this, according to the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for a criminal offence like this to be reported, regardless of the fact whether the perpetrator was known or unknown.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But given the situation on the ground and in this area there was no prosecutor to speak of, you would agree with me that in the absence of a Prosecutor there was no one to pass this information on to?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that strikes me as only logical, no prosecutor, no one to pass the information on to.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If this potential perpetrator, this man referred to as Mirzet, died within a time period of three months, do you agree with me when I say that our criminal law did not provide for a criminal proceedings to be initiated against someone who is dead?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You are absolutely right. Guilty or not, you can't try a dead man.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You testified about the communications with Tuzla. You said that between the corps and Srebrenica, such communications barely existed before the time of demilitarisation. Or you said perhaps the second half of April 1994.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, or rather June 1994. I prefer to set that time frame. At any rate there were no communications?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If in Srebrenica itself, the highest level body was the War Presidency, the highest authority was the War Presidency and if the War Presidency was informed about this incident at the time it occurred, do you believe that this would have meant that the highest possible authority in the area was in fact informed?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time the War Presidency of Srebrenica municipality was indeed the highest form of civilian government, of civilian authority. And if this body was informed, this would have accounted to complying with one's duty to report on a possible criminal -- to report a possible criminal offence or the possibility that a criminal offence was committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, I would like now to read out a different section of this interview conducted with our client. If we could just please have this relevant portion distributed, if I could have the usher's assistance in distributing the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While we are waiting, can you give a specific indication which part --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be reading this out. Your Honours, this is V 02920. The tape number is 20 and the page number is 21. It's down towards the bottom of the page and as we are waiting for this to be distributed, I'll just start.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, what we have here is the English version of the text and if the interpreters could please follow. We can have the English version displayed on the ELMO. If that helps. If that's of any assistance. Please if we could have the English version on the ELMO and I'll be reading the statement to the witness in the Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Witness, it's down towards the bottom of the page. But what I wish to read you is the following -- "Jezercica [phoen] and Kravica, just for example. I'm just talking now about the part where I -- where we attacked the lines while we were fighting here in these trenches along the lines. The slope of the mountain is so steep and down at the bottom there is a plain, a clearing. It is flat land. We hadn't even taken half of this area and we could see that the civilians had already moved into the village. So please, if you can explain to me how I was supposed to exercise control over the people who were in the midst of these houses. If there is an expert alive anywhere in the world who could show me how this should have been done, then they might as well hang me right away. Please bear in mind the fact that Chetniks were all over the place and surrounding the enclave. I had to hold the line right there to prevent them from coming in and killing our civilians." And then we'll move on to a different portion. "When you bear this in mind please also bear in mind the lie of the land and the very area in which this attacked occurred. Then you have to calculate how many soldiers I should have needed for this. They needn't necessarily have been armed. They would just be standing there without weapons, linking hands, to form a cordon to prevent civilians to leaving. In the meantime the combat was going on. What idiot is going to stand in front of a line like that to prevent people from coming in when they simply could have been shot from the back? Please bear in mind the fact that there was cannibalism at the time. People were starving. I wonder if there is anyone alive who could tell me how I was supposed to run this. If there is they might as well lock me up for 300 years and shoot me." Witness, -- witness, in relation to this, did you ever hear that there was cannibalism in Srebrenica in early January 1993, that there were incidents of cannibalism? Is this something that you were aware of? Did you know that people were starving there?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. We did know. There was some information that seeped through the information channels and this is the sort of information that reached Tuzla generally speaking, which was the -- where the headquarters for this district was based. As well as the corps command. This is the type of information that did eventually reach us. We knew that people were serving, that there was a general shortage of just about everything and that it was a question of bare survival. If you ask about the lie of the land, the terrain is very difficult. I'm familiar with the area. I was there -- I used to go there for a couple of years before the war so I'm familiar with the area. It's very difficult terrain. Very forbidding and the winters are severe, if I may put it that way. You usually get deep snow and extremely low temperatures. So whenever this sort of information reached us, we would just hold our heads in despair, not knowing what to do because we ourselves were short on what was necessary and what we needed to send them, and we didn't know how to deliver this to Srebrenica. The nearest point after the fall of Cerska and Konjevic Polje, the nearest point inside the free territory under the control of the BH army and the part of territory under control of the Srebrenica OG, the nearest point, I'd say, was at a distance of 36 kilometres. In wintertime conditions, you needed to cover all that ground. It was next to impossible. Your trail could be seen and our opposition was a very powerful forms on to their teeth and no courier would have stood a chance because they were in a position to catch up with anyone and track down anyone. There were situations where couriers went missing on the way to Srebrenica and were never found again. If the Chamber could forgive me for this elaboration, but there was a whole squad of reconnaissance officers who were killed until a bid to get through to Srebrenica. The period of time when Cerska fell, I believe that was on the 8th of March 1992, we tried something like that but the plan fell through on account of the deep snow, on account of the winter temperatures, and on account of the very few fighters that we had who were available for a mission like that. And there was a problem taken is very seriously. What we were trying to do is to preserve the Srebrenica, to make sure it could at least survive. Ms. Vidovic, if we go back to the did agreement on demilitarisation, do you know what that meant? That amounted to capitulation, to surrender. And this would have turned the enclave to a prisoner camp in no time at all. You know yourself all too well what happened later on in 1995. Please forgive me for being so extensive.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much but I do have a question in connection with this. Just one question. It's true, isn't it, that our regulations did not require that any commander should try to do the impossible; would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, that's a very fair statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before my learned friend from the OTP resumes her examination, can I please ask that this witness not be asked any leading questions on re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What are we going to do with this extract? Shall we give it a number?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please, Your Honours. My apologies. Thank you very much for drawing my attention to that. Can we please have a number assigned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Defence number D281. Yes, short re-examination, Ms. Sellers, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, you've been asked questions concerning the chain of command of the military police during the re-examination by learned friend Madam Vidovic. And among the things that you stated was that you need to have a clear chain of command and the ability for a police office to function. The first question I'd like to put to you is that if there were police units or officers operating in Srebrenica, even outside of the regulations that you're familiar with from 2 Corps, would those police units -- or is it possible those police units would form among themselves some type of command structure?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Civilian police or military police?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Let me clarify, the military police. But there was discussion on both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it -- I noticed precisely what you raised, but I take it that it was clear from the beginning of the question that we are talking of military police and not civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, excuse me. If we can answer the question. Would it be possible those police units could form among themselves some type of command structure?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question. Are we -- are we looking at military police units or civilian police units?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm talking about military police units. And even if they operated outside of the regulations of 2 Corps, is it possible that the police units formed some type of structure among themselves?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I simply don't understand the question. If there is a unit, then the unit presumably has a commander. I'm not sure about this term, "among themselves," what exactly you mean by "among themselves." So this is the specific part of your question that I'm not clear about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers, if you are aware of any such informal command structure created by military police units amongst themselves that you could ask the witness about, then go ahead with your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, in the summer of 1992, the formation of some of the TO structures -- or some of the TO structures, you testified, operated outside of the regulations of 2nd Corps. And within the formation of some of those TO structures is the possibility that police units were also part of the structure. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. It's a possibility. The whole of Srebrenica and the entire defence structure was a matter of improvisation, I'd say, to a large extent.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'd like to show Mr. Hogic Prosecution Exhibit 11, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we could please at least have the document placed on the ELMO so we can follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Thank you, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The document is on Sanction, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask Mr. Hogic to look over the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, does this document reflect what could be a structure between the TO and the military police in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It talks about the organisational structure of the military police from battalion level up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would you look and see the person's position who signed the document. Would you agree with me that that's a person who is related to the military structure, to the TO structure or the armed forces structure?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The signature belongs to the Chief of Staff of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can remove the document. I'd like now in that same vein to show Mr. Hogic Prosecution Exhibit P80, please. Your Honour, I believe that will be coming up on Sanction also. Your Honour, might I ask, there was a word that appeared in the transcript. I'm not certain of what it meant. It says "provakas." I didn't recognise it in English. That was with Mr. Hogic's answer to my question prior to showing him the previous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which line?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It is now off our current screen. And it was his answer to my question in terms of the structures. And I assume that the word he meant was improvisation but it was in -- a bit indiscernible. I just want to draw the attention to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you are referring to page 84, line 4, that's what I have, "improvisation."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know if you are referring to some other line.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't see it at this moment. I think improvisation is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you asked, then, to have Exhibit 11 shown to the witness so it must be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, the document you have in front of you comes, and you can see on the signature page, from Nedzad Behtic, the man we have been discussing in prior documents. It's dated the 19th of September 1993 and addressed to the 2nd Corps command. And if you look through the document it seems to be a resume of structures, whether the structures are within or without the legal framework. I would like to point you to, in the English it would be page 3, and it follows from the first formation structure. And under Section 10, there is a line that says "OS Srebrenica Military Police, 67 Conscripts Commanded by Mirzet Halilovic." Would you agree that the document appears to reflect that that's part of the Srebrenica Territorial Defence formations?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, the nature of these questions are all leading, essentially. I mean they are also speculative because we are talking about possible structures and things which this witness isn't being asked about his own knowledge, but to show parts of documents and say do you agree that this reflects, and then putting a proposition is clearly a leading way of conducting the re-examination. My learned friends can say does this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right, Mr. Jones. Please rephrase the question, me. There is an easy way of putting it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, after looking through that part of the document what would that reflect to you in terms of the military police?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document talking about the formation structure or establishing a structure of the armed forces of Srebrenica. The first time this occurred was on the 20th of May 1992. That's what the document says. And the next time was on the 3rd of September 1992. I haven't had time to go through the entire document to see if there is anything else. The third establishment was in mid-December 1992, it appears to suggest.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, if I might, thank you, now draw your attention under the first establishment, under number 10. "Services Attached to OS Srebrenica," where it says "OS Srebrenica, Military Police 67 conscripts, Commander Mirzet Halilovic."

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And your comment on that in relationship to your understanding of the document?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that at this point in time, at least based on this document, there was a military police unit that had been organised comprising this number of conscripts. That's in as far as the document is accurate and I have no reason to assume otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would ask you to stay with us in the same document, it would be page 7, in the English version, it is now under what you have previously testified to being the second formation structure of the 3rd of September 1992, and there is a number 9, starting a paragraph, and then in that paragraph, we go to number 15. If you would read number 15. "Military Police Commander Mirzet Halilovic" and then the paragraph under it, "Units 9 through 15 including members of the staff total 323 conscripts." "The Srebrenica armed forces of the 2nd formation structure number 53, 5.312 conscripts," your comment on what that would indicate, please.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time there was some kind of a military police unit commanded by Mirzet Halilovic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. And then could I ask you, it would be page 8 in the English version. It is an English version prior to the signature page, and it deals with, as you've testified before, a subsequent formation, from mid-December 1992 under section 3. And then I would ask you to go to the last paragraph prior to section 4. Towards the bottom of that paragraph it says, "The staff appointed Akif the commander of Srebrenica OS military police on the 22nd of November 1992." And if you would glance just above that paragraph in reference to the staff, it appears to be "members of the Srebrenica OS increased in the third formation." Your comment on that, please.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here it says that all the units remained organised in accordance with the previous organization. They continued to function but certain changes were made. It also refers to the number of men et cetera, and then believe me I can't read everything, but it says that from the 5th of February 1993, certain people in certain posts were changed. This Mandic Smaijlo [phoen] was in a certain post and Mehmedovic was also the assistant chief of training and operations, and as of the 16th of April 1993 there were some new individuals. Then there was Bogilovic Becir, who was the assistant -- the chief of intelligence and security issues and from the 29th of April 1993 that position was taken by Nedzad Behtic. So these were the positions that members of the staff of the Srebrenica armed forces had. They had been appointed to these positions by virtue of certain documents. I assume issued by the commander of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
